title: Disruption in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about how markets change: old technologies that refuse to die, new ones that take over, and the market leaders caught in between.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Change is rarely as fast, or as slow, as we expect.
paras: Some of today's numbers moved much faster than most people guessed: whole product categories shrank to a fraction of their size within a decade. Others barely moved at all, and old habits are still with us years after they were declared dead.
Telling the two apart in advance is one of the hardest jobs in business, and confident predictions in either direction are often wrong.

questions.q: In 1964, a company in America's S&P 500 index of large firms stayed in it for 33 years on average. For companies in the index by 2027, the consultancy Innosight forecast an average of...
questions.explain: Innosight forecast that the average stay would shrink to about 12 years by 2027, roughly a third of the 1964 figure. Firms leave the index when they are overtaken, taken over or bought by private equity, so a place among the giants is far less secure than it used to be. This is a forecast based on past trends, not a measured result.
questions.source: Innosight, 2018 Corporate Longevity Forecast (reported by Governance Intelligence)

questions.q: What share of the world's recorded music revenue came from streaming in 2025?
questions.explain: Streaming brought in more than US$22 billion of the industry's US$31.7 billion, almost 70% of the total. Global revenue grew for the eleventh year in a row, after a long collapse in CD sales in the 2000s. Physical formats grew too: vinyl sales rose for the 19th year running.

questions.q: Bitkom, Germany's digital industry association, surveyed companies with 20 or more employees in 2025. What share still use a fax machine regularly?
questions.explain: Fewer than one in five German companies still fax regularly, a sharp fall from 33% in 2023 and 30% in 2024. For years the fax survived in Germany long after most countries had moved on, often because public offices, doctors or legal rules still expected it.

questions.q: In 2025, what share of new passenger cars registered in Norway were fully electric?
questions.explain: Almost every new car sold in Norway in 2025 was battery-electric: 172,233 out of 179,550. Norway had set a target that all new cars should be zero-emission by 2025, and it used heavy taxes on petrol and diesel cars, with exemptions for electric ones, to get there.
questions.source: Norwegian Road Federation (OFV), registrations 2025, reported by electrive, January 2026

questions.q: In 2010, a record 121.5 million digital cameras were shipped worldwide. How many were shipped in 2025?
questions.explain: Shipments fell by more than 90% in fifteen years, as smartphone cameras became good enough for almost everyone. Surprisingly, 2025 was a six-year high, up 11% on 2024, and the value of shipments was the highest in ten years: fewer cameras are sold, but they are more expensive.
questions.source: Camera & Imaging Products Association (CIPA), shipment statistics 2010 and 2025

questions.q: The Bundesbank records how people in Germany pay for everyday purchases. In 2025, what share of payments (by number) were made in cash?
questions.explain: Cash was still used for 45% of purchases, more than any other single method, but for the first time most payments (55%) were cashless. Debit cards came second with 26% and mobile payments reached 10%. Two years earlier cash had still been used for just over half of all payments.
questions.source: Deutsche Bundesbank, Payment behaviour in Germany 2025 (published June 2026)

questions.q: In 2008, a year after the first iPhone went on sale, what share of all mobile phones sold worldwide were made by Nokia?
questions.explain: Nokia sold almost four in ten of the 1.2 billion or so phones sold worldwide in 2008, far more than any rival. Within a few years smartphones had changed the market, and in 2014 Nokia sold its phone business to Microsoft.
questions.source: ABI Research, 2008 market share figures (reported by All About Symbian); Gartner, 2008 handset sales

questions.q: How many people paid for a music streaming subscription worldwide in 2025?
questions.explain: IFPI counted 837 million users of paid subscription accounts, and paid subscriptions alone made up more than half of all recorded music revenue. Twenty years ago, paying a monthly fee for music you never own would have sounded like a strange business model.
